findings.headline: Sheerness Revival Levelling Up Fund project entering final delivery stage within budget and reporting schedule
findings.detail: The Sheerness Revival LUF project is in its final stages of delivery with completion planned for Autumn 2026. Current forecasts are within budget and reporting deadlines are up to date.
findings.matters: Timely delivery of capital schemes, particularly government-funded ones, demonstrates project management capability and is relevant to both lenders and peer councils in similar programs
findings.figures: Autumn 2026
findings.quote: The project is now entering the final stages of delivery with a planned completion date of Autumn 2026. Current forecasts are within budget and reporting deadlines are up to date.

findings.headline: Government announced pause in Local Government Reorganisation; Swale's reorganisation direction remains uncertain
findings.detail: Swale's full council endorsed its preferred geography option for LGR on 19 November, following submission of proposed options by Kent councils. However, the government announced a pause of the LGR process in September 2026, and further activity is now dependent on the government's decision review outcome.
findings.matters: LGR creates uncertainty about the council's future structure, funding allocation and operations, making medium-term financial planning difficult
findings.quote: In September 2026 the government announced a pause of LGR, so further activity is dependent on the outcome of the decision review.

findings.headline: Homelessness funding settlement reduced for 2026/27 despite one-off compensatory grant; underlying formula penalizes deprived areas
findings.detail: The finance settlement for 2026/27 contained an anomaly resulting in reduced homelessness funding for Swale. A one-off grant for one year was awarded to compensate for late notification of the cut. However, the council states the underlying homelessness funding formula appears to penalize the most deprived areas and continues to lobby government on this issue.
findings.matters: Homelessness is a statutory duty; a formula that penalizes deprived areas creates ongoing structural underfunding that management cannot control
findings.figures: one-off, one year grant
findings.quote: An apparent anomaly in the finance settlement for 2026/27 saw a reduction in homelessness funding for Swale. A one off, one year grant has been awarded to compensate for the late notification of the reduction, but the underlying formula for homelessness funding appears to penalise the most deprived areas – an issue that we continue to lobby government on to address.

findings.headline: Final government finance settlement removed business rate growth, leaving £1.2m budget shortfall for 2027/28
findings.detail: The local government finance settlement for 2026/27 eliminated all business rate growth from the council's funding. While most of this loss was offset by increased Revenue Support Grant, a net reduction of £1.2m remains. The council must address this budget gap in the 2027/28 budget build to deliver a balanced budget.
findings.matters: An unresolved £1.2m budget gap indicates the council faces significant spending cuts or income measures needed to balance the 2027/28 budget
findings.quote: The outcome of the final settlement has removed all business rate growth from our funding settlement. Whilst most had been compensated by an increase in RSG a reduction of £1.2m remains. The 2027/28 budget build process will need to address the ongoing budget gap to deliver a balanced budget.

findings.headline: External Audit gave except for qualification opinion on 2024/25 accounts for accounting treatment of capital expenditure in 2023/24
findings.detail: Grant Thornton's audit of the 2024/25 financial statements resulted in an 'except for qualification' opinion relating to the accounting treatment of capital expenditure in the prior year (2023/24). Although the treatment had net zero impact on the financial position, work is ongoing on the audit recommendations.
findings.matters: An audit qualification on capital expenditure accounting indicates control weaknesses in the accounting framework and raises questions about the reliability of financial reporting
findings.figures: net zero impact on the financial position
findings.quote: During 2025/26 the External Audit of 2024/25 was completed by Grant Thornton, an except for qualification opinion was given on the main audit with regards to the accounting treatment of capital expenditure in 2023/24. There was net zero impact on the financial position as a result of the treatment.

findings.headline: Temporary accommodation costs rose significantly, contributing to housing and community services overspend of £296k
findings.detail: Temporary accommodation—emergency housing for homeless and at-risk households—incurred material cost increases. This was partially offset by additional grants and contributions. The overspend contributed to the broader Housing and Community Services variance of £296k.
findings.matters: Temporary accommodation cost spikes reflect homelessness and housing crisis pressures; this demand-driven cost signals acute social need and material budget risk affecting council financial sustainability.
findings.figures: Housing & Community overspend £296k; budget £4,421k against spend of £4,718k
findings.quote: The cost of temporary accommodation has significantly increased. This has been partly offset by additional grants and contributions.

findings.headline: Total borrowing increased £4.1m from £13m to £17.1m, including £3m of new long-term loans at 4.86% weighted average rate
findings.detail: Swale moved from holding only short-term loans to a mixed maturity portfolio. Long-term borrowing increased from zero to £3m, borrowed from local authorities and PWLB. Capital funding records show £1.439m was borrowed for capital projects; the deployment of the additional £2.7m increase is not explained in this extract.
findings.matters: A £4.1m increase in outstanding debt is material and affects debt servicing and future borrowing capacity; the shift to long-term borrowing and incomplete transparency on purposes merit lender and peer scrutiny.
findings.figures: Total borrowing: £13m (31 March 2025) to £17.1m (31 March 2026); long-term loans: £0 to £3m; seven loans, each £2-3m; weighted average rate 4.86%
findings.quote: At 31 March 2026, the Council had seven loans, totalling £17.1 million, each ranging in value from £2 million to £3 million, from local authorities and the PWLB, at a weighted average interest rate of 4.86%.

findings.headline: Collection Fund swung to £0.917m deficit from £0.1m surplus, a deterioration of approximately £1m year-on-year
findings.detail: The Collection Fund—which holds council tax and business rates pending distribution to the council and preceptors—moved from a small surplus to a material deficit. The cause is not explained in this extract, but the swing suggests either lower-than-expected tax collection or economic stress affecting collection rates in the area.
findings.matters: The Collection Fund deficit directly affects the council's cash position and available resources; a £1m swing signals collection challenges or underlying economic stress that lenders and peer councils monitor.
findings.figures: Collection Fund £0.917m deficit at 31 March 2026 (£0.1m surplus at 31 March 2025); swing of £1.017m
findings.quote: At the year-end, this account had a deficit balance of £0.917 million (surplus balance of £0.1m at 31 March 2025).

findings.headline: Capital programme slippage of £21.054m into 2026/27, principally from delays to the affordable homes scheme
findings.detail: The council deferred £21.054m of planned capital spending into 2026/27. The primary driver is delays to the affordable homes scheme. Additional slippage reflects the revised timeline for the Levelling Up Sheerness Revival project. This affects both capital delivery rates and project affordability planning.
findings.matters: A £21m capital slippage materially affects programme execution and debt capacity; delays to affordable housing signal broader housing delivery challenges facing councils.
findings.figures: Capital slippage £21.054m into 2026/27; total capital spend 2025/26 was £14.8m
findings.quote: Due to delays and reprofiling of capital projects, there will be slippage of £21.054m into 2026/27. The reason for the slippage is mainly due to delays to the affordable homes scheme.

findings.headline: Planning service overspent by £570k in 2025/26, driven by agency staffing costs outpacing vacancy savings and reduced fee income
findings.detail: The planning service incurred a £570k overspend. The cost of agency staff hired to fill vacancies exceeded the savings generated by unfilled posts. Planning fee income fell short of budget due to fewer applications received. The council is continuing recruitment efforts to shift toward permanent staffing and control costs.
findings.matters: A material, recurring service cost pressure that shows staffing challenges affecting service delivery and budget stability—a challenge replicated across other councils.
findings.figures: Planning overspend £570k; budget £1,203k against spend of £1,773k
findings.quote: The overspend is due to the cost of the agency staff outstripping the savings from the vacancies and reduced planning fees income as a result of fewer planning applications.

findings.headline: Unqualified audit opinion issued with no statutory recommendations, Public Interest Reports, or use of auditor formal powers; prior-year risk management recommendation withdrawn
findings.detail: The Council received an unqualified (clean) audit opinion on its 2025/26 financial statements following the Audit Committee meeting on 14 October 2026. No issues were identified that required statutory recommendations, Public Interest Reports, or applications for judicial review. The Annual Governance Statement was not found to be misleading or inconsistent with audit findings. The prior-year improvement recommendation on mapping corporate risks to strategic objectives has been withdrawn, as the Council has now implemented a revised risk management framework that properly aligns risks to corporate objectives.
findings.matters: A clean audit opinion and absence of use of formal auditor powers indicates no identified accounting or governance failures; the lifting of a prior recommendation shows incremental improvement in governance practice and risk management alignment with strategy.
findings.figures: None
findings.quote: We plan to issue an unqualified opinion on the Council's financial statements following the Audit Committee meeting on 14 October 2026.

findings.headline: Government pause to Local Government Reorganisation decisions (announced 7 September 2026) defers clarity on Kent four-unitary proposal, extending period of planning uncertainty for the Council
findings.detail: On 7 September 2026, the government announced a pause to Local Government Reorganisation decisions for most geographies (Essex, Suffolk, Norfolk, Hampshire decisions were withdrawn; other LGR geographies paused). The Council had submitted a Strategic Business Case in November 2025 ahead of the government's July 2026 announcement of a four-unitary proposal for Kent with no boundary changes. The deferral extends the period of uncertainty about future council boundaries, structures, and funding implications. The Council has cited this uncertainty as a reason for not finalising multi-year savings plans, though the government's pause now provides some clarity that reorganisation will not occur before at least April 2028.
findings.matters: LGR creates capacity demands and planning uncertainty for all councils in affected geographies; finance directors in LGR-affected areas must manage two-year cycles of reorganisation planning alongside business-as-usual service delivery and financial sustainability; the pause deferring decisions provides some relief but extends the overall uncertainty period.
findings.figures: Government pause announced 7 September 2026; originally proposed vesting date April 2028; Shadow Authority elections originally May 2027
findings.quote: On 7 September 2026 the government announced a pause to LGR decisions. The decisions relating to Essex, Suffolk, Norfolk and Hampshire (originally announced on 26 March 2026) have been withdrawn. For other LGR geographies, the government's decisions announced on 16 July 2026 are paused and are to be reviewed.

findings.headline: Cockleshell Walk housing development (51 new social rented homes) proceeding to construction funded through prudential borrowing, capital receipts, and Homes England grant against backdrop of reserve depletion
findings.detail: The Cockleshell Walk scheme is being funded through a combination of capital receipts (including Section 106 funds), Homes England grant funding, reserves, and prudential borrowing. The development has progressed to construction following planning permission and land appropriation. This represents the only one of three original sites in the Swale Rainbow Homes Ltd affordable housing programme to have reached construction; the other two sites remain paused. The decision to borrow for this project occurs during a period when the Council forecasts reserve depletion and has not yet identified formal savings to close future budget gaps.
findings.matters: A lending authority monitors the council's leverage position and its capacity to service debt; borrowing to fund capital at a time of reserve depletion and unresolved future budget gaps represents a judgement call about risk that lenders assess alongside the council's overall debt burden and liquidity trajectory.
findings.figures: Cockleshell Walk: 51 new social rented homes; funded by capital receipts, grant, reserves and prudential borrowing; reserves to decline to £6.5m by 2029/30
findings.quote: The Cockleshell Walk development is being funded through a combination of capital receipts and prudential borrowing.

findings.headline: 2025/26 revenue underspend of £579k masks underlying service pressures in Planning (£570k overspend) and Housing (£296k overspend), offset by one-time corporate overhead savings
findings.detail: The Council achieved a £579k revenue underspend at year-end. The underspend was primarily driven by a £1.4m underspend in Corporate Overheads and Capital Financing, arising from higher than budgeted investment income, reduced pension backfunding contributions, insurance savings, and surplus budget provisions. These savings were offset by service level pressures, including a £570k overspend in Planning and a £296k overspend in Housing and Community Services. The Planning overspend arose from recruitment challenges and reduced planning fee income; the Housing overspend arose from increasing homelessness and temporary accommodation costs. The audit noted these pressures were understood and actively managed.
findings.matters: While the aggregate position shows underspend, the composition reveals ongoing demand-driven service pressures (homelessness, temporary accommodation) that may persist or grow, and reliance on corporate-level savings that may not repeat; a peer finance director would want to understand whether the 2025/26 position masks weaker underlying structural finances.
findings.figures: Overall underspend: £579k; reserve draw: £581k (vs £1.16m budgeted); Corporate overhead savings: £1.4m; Planning overspend: £570k; Housing overspend: £296k
findings.quote: The Council achieved a £579k revenue underspend at year-end. The underspend was primarily driven by a £1.4m underspend in Corporate Overheads and Capital Financing. These savings were offset by service level pressures, including a £570k overspend in Planning and a £296k overspend in Housing and Community Services.

findings.headline: Capital programme slippage of £21.1m in 2025/26, plus £14.7m carried from prior year, primarily in affordable housing due to construction inflation and funding viability challenges
findings.detail: The Council reported a £21.1m capital programme underspend, reprofiled into 2026/27, following £14.7m of slippage carried forward from 2024/25. The largest element relates to the Affordable Homes Programme (Swale Rainbow Homes Ltd), where the Council originally planned three sites but only Cockleshell Walk has progressed to construction. The other two sites remain paused. Delays arose from construction cost inflation, increased borrowing costs, the need to secure additional external funding to restore scheme viability, and contractor procurement issues.
findings.matters: Capital delays of this scale over two consecutive years affect the council's ability to deliver strategic objectives and create ongoing budget pressures; for lenders, persistent slippage indicates project delivery risk and potential need for revised borrowing strategies.
findings.figures: 2025/26 slippage: £21.1m; prior-year slippage carried forward: £14.7m; total cumulative slippage: £35.8m; Cockleshell Walk scheme: 51 new social rented homes
findings.quote: The Council reported a £21.1m capital programme underspend, reprofiled into 2026/27, following £14.7m of slippage carried forward from 2024/25. The most significant element relates to the Affordable Homes Programme, where delays arose from construction cost inflation, increased borrowing costs, the need to secure additional external funding to restore scheme viability

findings.headline: Funding gaps of £7.3m projected across 2026/27 to 2029/30 with no formal long-term savings programme established despite prior-year audit recommendation
findings.detail: The MTFS identifies budget gaps of £459k in 2026/27, rising to £1.430m in 2027/28, £2.958m in 2028/29, and £2.489m in 2029/30. For 2026/27, savings of £1.2m have been identified, leaving a remaining gap of £459k to be funded from reserves. However, the Council has not yet developed quantified savings plans for 2027/28 to 2029/30 or established a formal long-term savings programme, despite this being recommended by auditors in 2024/25. Management cited uncertainty from the absence of multi-year funding settlements and the evolution of Local Government Reorganisation as barriers to longer-term planning.
findings.matters: Finance directors and lenders assess sustainability by examining whether councils have identified concrete solutions to closing identified gaps; the absence of a formal programme for three-quarters of the planning period, combined with declining reserves, represents material financial sustainability risk.
findings.quote: Given the Council's planned reliance on reserves and the absence of identified savings proposals beyond 2026/27, we reiterate our recommendation that the Council develop a formal, medium-term savings programme to support financial sustainability.

findings.headline: Total usable reserves forecast to fall from £22.1m to £6.5m by March 2029, reducing financial resilience over the medium term
findings.detail: The Council's MTFS forecasts significant reserve depletion over the three-year period from 31 March 2026 to 31 March 2029. Earmarked reserves are projected to reduce from £19.08m to £3.42m, and total usable reserves from £22.18m to £6.52m, with the general fund held at £3.1m throughout. This depletion is driven by planned use of reserves to fund budget gaps identified in the MTFS, alongside service pressures including homelessness and temporary accommodation costs.
findings.matters: A lending council or finance director assessing creditworthiness watches reserve trajectories as indicators of financial sustainability and capacity to absorb shocks; reserves depleting to £6.5m represent materially reduced liquidity within the medium-term planning period.
findings.figures: Reserves: £22.18m (31 March 2026) to £6.52m (31 March 2029); earmarked reserves: £19.08m to £3.42m; general fund: £3.1m throughout
findings.quote: earmarked reserves reducing from £19.08m to £3.42m and total usable reserves from £22.18m to £6.52m by 2028/29

findings.headline: Asset valuation errors totalling £395k identified during audit but not corrected by management.
findings.detail: Auditors identified two asset valuation errors: investment property understated by £109k because the valuer was not provided with updated rental agreements, and right-of-use asset (Car Forum Park) understated by £286k because incorrect income data was submitted by the Council. Both items individually exceed the £85k reporting threshold. Management chose not to adjust these errors on grounds that they were immaterial and that making late changes to the accounts posed higher risk of introducing additional mistakes.
findings.matters: Asset valuation errors indicate process issues in how management communicates changes to valuers and manages source data quality; whilst immaterial at balance-sheet level here, they signal control weaknesses in data governance.
findings.figures: £109k investment property understatement; £286k right-of-use asset understatement; total £395k unadjusted.
findings.quote: We identified, for one sample tested, that the rental passing considered in the valuation workbook did not agree with the actual rental agreement resulting in increase of £109k in the valuation of investment property. We identified, for the Car Forum Park asset, that the income considered for the right-of-use asset valuation was incorrect due to wrong data submitted by the Council. This resulted in the right-of-use asset balance being understated by £286k.

findings.headline: Gross expenditure decreased 12% year-on-year, triggering downward revision of materiality from £2m to £1.7m.
findings.detail: The Council's gross expenditure decreased 12% compared to the prior year, a significant year-on-year reduction. This change prompted the auditors to revise materiality downward from the planning figure of £2m to £1.7m, based on 2.5% of revised gross expenditure. The paper does not explain the drivers of this expenditure reduction. Such a material swing would typically reflect either planned efficiency gains or significant service/activity reductions.
findings.matters: A 12% year-on-year expenditure reduction is material to understanding the Council's financial trajectory and sustainability; lenders and peer councils would need to understand whether this reflects deliberate efficiency, service rationalisation, or other factors.
findings.figures: 12% decrease in gross expenditure; materiality revised from £2.0m to £1.7m; performance materiality from £1.4m to £1.275m.
findings.quote: The downward revision is a result of an overall decrease in Council's gross expenditure of 12% from the prior year.

findings.headline: Five of nine prior-year audit recommendations remain open, including £3.1m of fully depreciated assets still in use.
findings.detail: Of nine recommendations from the 2024/25 audit, four have been closed and five remain open. Open items include identification of three peppercorn leases (£134k combined), reclassification of one PPE asset, reassessment of fully depreciated assets still in use (£3.1m), employee benefits FTE reconciliation, and reconciliation of transaction listings. The persistence of these items over a full year suggests either management does not view them as material/urgent or capacity constraints exist.
findings.matters: The number of open prior-year recommendations is an indicator of management's capacity and prioritisation; five items remaining open after a full year signals either risk tolerance or resource limitations in the finance function.
findings.figures: £134k peppercorn leases; £3.1m fully depreciated assets; 5 of 9 prior-year recommendations still open.
findings.quote: We identified the following issues in the audit of the Council's 2024/25 financial statements, which resulted in 9 recommendations reported in our 2024/25 Audit Findings Report. 4 of these recommendations are now closed and 5 remain open.

findings.headline: Long-term savings programme recommendation carried forward from prior year without sufficient progress.
findings.detail: The auditors' value for money assessment carried forward a recommendation from 2024/25 regarding establishment of a long-term savings programme, noting insufficient progress has been made to address it. This second consecutive carry-forward suggests either the savings challenge remains unresolved or management has not prioritised the recommendation. The auditors remain satisfied overall that the Council has proper arrangements for economy, efficiency and effectiveness, but the recommendation highlights budget or implementation challenges requiring attention.
findings.matters: A carry-forward VFM recommendation in consecutive years signals potential budget pressures or implementation capacity gaps; peer councils and lenders monitor whether councils deliver on self-identified improvements.
findings.figures: No figures.
findings.quote: we have carried forward one improvement recommendation from the prior year regarding the establishment of a long-term savings programme, as insufficient progress has been made to fully address the recommendation

findings.headline: Shared journal user IDs identified in testing; remediated through new finance system implementation.
findings.detail: During testing of management override of controls, the auditors identified two instances where user accounts were not uniquely assigned: one employee held two user IDs, and a system administrator account was shared between two individuals. These arrangements reduce user accountability and weaken the audit trail by preventing reliable attribution of journal activity to individuals. Management has responded that all users now have unique IDs per staff member in the newly implemented finance system.
findings.matters: User accountability in financial systems is fundamental to internal control; whilst remediated, this represents a control weakness that persisted into 2025/26.
findings.figures: No figures.
findings.quote: During our testing, we identified the following instances where user accounts were not uniquely assigned to individual users: one individual assigned two user IDs, and a system administrator account shared between two individuals.

findings.headline: Property, plant and equipment revaluation approach departs from CIPFA Code requirements.
findings.detail: The Council has adopted an annual formal revaluation approach for high-value assets, rather than the CIPFA Code requirement for either quinquennial revaluation with annual indexation or a rolling five-year programme with indexation. Management has defended the departure on grounds that annual revaluations produce more accurate valuations. The auditors' review concluded the PPE valuation was not materially misstated despite the Code non-compliance, but have raised a medium-priority recommendation requiring realignment with the Code.
findings.matters: Departure from the Code signals a willingness to prioritise alternative approaches over compliance requirements; peer councils and lenders assess governance culture through such choices.
findings.figures: Disclosure variances identified: £133k for Land and Buildings, £151k for Assets Under Construction, and £17k for Surplus Assets.
findings.quote: Management adopted an annual formal revaluation approach for high-value assets, rather than the valuation approach prescribed by the CIPFA Code which came into effect from 2025/26. This is a departure from the Code requirements.

findings.headline: Audit certificate cannot be formally closed pending public objection resolution and NAO Whole of Government Accounts certification.
findings.detail: The audit work is substantially complete with an unmodified opinion anticipated. However, the formal audit certificate cannot be issued until confirmation is received from the NAO that the Whole of Government Accounts group audit has been certified by the Comptroller and Auditor General, and the formal resolution of a public objection raised in respect of the 2025/26 accounts is concluded. The auditors note this outstanding work does not have a material effect on the financial statements.
findings.matters: A lender requires audited accounts before disbursing credit; a delayed certificate affects the timeline for full accounts approval and publication and is unusual.
findings.figures: No figures.
findings.quote: We cannot formally conclude the audit and issue an audit certificate in accordance with the requirements of the Local Audit and Accountability Act 2014 and the Code of Audit Practice until: confirmation is received from the NAO that the group audit (Whole of Government Accounts) has been certified by the Comptroller and Auditor General, and the formal resolution of the objection raised by a member of the public in respect of the 2025/26 accounts.

findings.headline: £286k Forum Car Park right-of-use asset valuation error identified; income data used in valuation was incorrect
findings.detail: Auditors found that the income data submitted by Swale Borough Council for valuing the Forum Car Park right-of-use asset was incorrect, resulting in the asset being understated by £286k. This error was not corrected in the final accounts for the same reason as the investment property error: the adjustment was not material and late changes risked introducing further errors.
findings.matters: Income data errors in asset valuations indicate potential data quality issues in the council's asset management and valuation processes, affecting lender understanding of the reliability of asset values and the council's capacity to generate income from its assets.
findings.quote: We identified, for the Forum Car Park asset, that the income considered for the right-of-use asset valuation was incorrect due to wrong data submitted by SBC. This resulted in the right-of-use asset balance being understated by £286k.

findings.headline: £109k investment property valuation error identified; rental agreement data in valuation workbook did not match actual agreement
findings.detail: Auditors identified during their sample testing of investment property valuations that the rental income used in the valuation workbook was higher than the amount stated in the actual rental agreement, resulting in an overstatement of £109k. The council did not correct this error in the financial statements, determining it to be immaterial and preferring not to introduce the risk of further errors through late amendments.
findings.matters: Asset valuation errors suggest potential weaknesses in the council's property valuation processes or data validation controls, directly relevant to lender assessment of balance sheet quality and asset reliability.
findings.quote: We identified, for one sample tested, that the rental passing considered in the valuation workbook did not agree with the actual rental agreement resulting in increase of £109k in the valuation of investment property.

findings.paper_title: 2026 -27 Treasury Management Q1 report Audit Committee
findings.headline: 82% of £17m outstanding borrowing matures within 12 months, creating significant maturity concentration and refinancing risk.
findings.detail: At 30 June 2026, the council held £17m of external borrowing, of which £13.94m (82%) is due to mature within the next 12 months. The council acknowledges that short-term borrowing costs have remained elevated, with the average rate on all loans at 4.46% and short-dated market rates between 4.0% and 4.5%.
findings.matters: Lenders assess maturity profiles to evaluate refinancing risk; concentration of debt maturities means the council will face substantial borrowing requirements in the coming year and is exposed to changes in short-term market rates.
findings.figures: £13.94m of £17m total borrowing due within 12 months; average loan rate 4.46%; short-term borrowing available at 4.0–4.5%.
findings.quote: The Council's short-term borrowing cost has remained high with the currently high Base Rate and short-dated market rates. The average rate on the Council's loans at 30 June 2026 was 4.46%.

findings.paper_title: 2026 -27 Treasury Management Q1 report Audit Committee
findings.headline: Ratio of financing costs to net revenue rising to 9.99% by 2027/28, reflecting growing revenue burden of debt service.
findings.detail: The proportion of the council's net revenue budget required to meet financing costs on existing and planned debt is projected to rise significantly: from 6.36% in 2025/26 to 8.58% in 2026/27 and 9.99% in 2027/28. This increase reflects both higher total debt and potentially higher interest rates as planned borrowing takes place.
findings.matters: Shows the growing revenue impact of capital spending decisions; signals building affordability pressures as debt service claims a larger share of spending capacity.
findings.figures: Financing costs ratio: 2025/26 actual 6.36%, 2026/27 estimate 8.58%, 2027/28 estimate 9.99%. Financing costs: £2.45m (2025/26), £2.534m (2026/27), £2.94m (2027/28).
findings.quote: General Fund Total 6.36% 8.58% 9.99% 9.97%

findings.headline: Capital expenditure planned to more than double to £31.2m in 2026/27, with capital financing requirement projected to rise 29% to £80.5m.
findings.detail: The council's capital spending plan shows significant acceleration from £14.8m in 2025/26 to £31.2m planned for 2026/27, a jump of 111%. findings.matters: Lenders need to understand the capital plans and borrowing trajectory; peer councils track comparable investment programmes and the costs associated with them.

findings.headline: Internal audit delivered a sound assurance opinion with no qualifications on governance, risk management, and control
findings.detail: The Head of Audit Partnership's annual assurance report for 2024/25 concluded that the council's internal control, governance, and risk management arrangements provided sound assurance. The opinion carried no qualifications or reservations.
findings.matters: An unqualified internal audit opinion confirms the council's internal control environment is working effectively; a qualified opinion would signal control weaknesses that affect operational and financial risk.
findings.figures: 2024/25 opinion
findings.quote: The report concluded that the Head of Audit was able to provide sound assurance with no qualifications to the opinion.

findings.headline: External audit issued an unmodified opinion on the 2024/25 annual accounts with no major adjustments required
findings.detail: Grant Thornton's external audit of the 2024/25 annual financial report was issued with an unmodified opinion in October 2025. No major adjustments to the financial statements were required before approval.
findings.matters: An unmodified (clean) audit opinion on financial statements is fundamental to lender confidence in the council's financial data reliability and accounting controls.
findings.figures: 2024/25 audit issued October 2025
findings.quote: The report issued an unmodified audit opinion. This meant that no major adjustments were required to the Council's annual financial report.

findings.paper_title: Audit Committee - Annual Treasury Management Report 2025-26
findings.headline: £350k reserve maintained against possible non-extension of statutory override on pooled investment fund accounting beyond 2029
findings.detail: The council previously set aside £350k to mitigate the impact if the statutory override on accounting for gains and losses in pooled investment funds was not extended. Although the override may continue to April 2029, the council has decided to maintain this reserve against the risk of future extension denial.
findings.matters: Policy uncertainty on investment accounting treatment creates a contingent liability; the reserve protects against potential balance sheet volatility if the override lapses in 2029.
findings.figures: £350k reserve maintained
findings.quote: The Council had set up a reserve of £350k to mitigate the impact of the statutory override not being extended. In view of the fact that the override may not be extended past 2029 the authority has decided to maintain this reserve

findings.paper_title: Audit Committee - Annual Treasury Management Report 2025-26
findings.headline: Non-treasury commercial property portfolio of £3.98m generating 6.45% return but concentrated in 11 properties
findings.detail: The council holds a longstanding portfolio of 11 commercial investment properties within the borough, valued at £3.983m. These are held for commercial return (not treasury management) and generated £257k income in 2025-26. The 6.45% return exceeds treasury yields but represents concentrated local real estate exposure.

findings.detail: The strategy notes that given 'significant cuts to public expenditure and in particular to local government funding', the council's borrowing strategy must 'address the key issue of affordability without compromising the longer-term stability of the debt portfolio'. This flags that the council is under financial pressure and has limited headroom for cost overruns or adverse variances.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand whether affordability constraints will limit the council's capacity to service debt if revenues fall, costs rise, or capital costs overrun. The council's acknowledgment that affordability is a key concern suggests limited financial resilience.

findings.headline: Capital expenditure cliff of 89% between 2026/27 and 2027/28 with no explanation in strategy.
findings.detail: The council's capital programme jumps to £31.410m in 2026/27, requiring £22.234m of borrowing, but then drops to only £3.415m in 2027/28 and £4.319m in 2028/29. The strategy document does not explain whether this reflects completion of a specific multi-year scheme or anticipated funding constraints in future years.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand whether the council's capital plans are sustainable and predictable. A sharp, unexplained cliff in capital expenditure suggests either a one-off programme ending or emerging constraints on future capital capacity. This affects the council's long-term investment capability and revenue generation.

findings.headline: Council deliberately using short-term borrowing to save costs, exposing it to interest rate and refinancing risk.
findings.detail: The strategy explicitly chooses short-term loans over long-term fixed-rate borrowing, assuming this will be cheaper. New short-term loans are budgeted at 4.50%, compared to higher long-term rates. The council acknowledges that 'short-term and variable rate loans leave the Council exposed to the risk of short-term interest rate rises'. The strategy depends on interest rates falling and remaining low, and on the council retaining access to short-term refinancing when £12m matures.
findings.matters: This strategy creates material interest rate risk. If the Bank of England's rate forecasts prove incorrect and rates rise rather than fall, or if other councils become less willing to lend when Swale's loans mature, the cost of refinancing £12m plus borrowing £22.2m new could increase significantly.
findings.figures: New short-term loans assumed at average rate of 4.50%; existing loans at 4.25%–4.82%; Bank Rate forecast to reach 3.25% by end 2026
findings.quote: Short-term interest rates have fallen over the past year, and are expected to fall a little further, and it is therefore likely to be more cost effective over the medium-term to either use internal resources, or to borrow short-term loans instead. The risks of this approach will be managed by keeping the Council's interest rate exposure within the limit set in the treasury management prudential indicators.

findings.headline: £12m of existing loans all mature in Q2-Q3 2026, requiring refinancing in same year the council borrows £22.2m for capital.

Simultaneously, the council plans to borrow £22.234m for a £31.4m capital programme, meaning total refinancing and new borrowing needs of roughly £34m in one financial year.
findings.matters: A lender needs to assess refinancing risk. Concentrating £34m of borrowing needs into a single year, with all existing debt maturing simultaneously, creates significant execution risk if capital markets tighten or if refinancing appetite narrows.
findings.figures: £12m existing debt maturing April-September 2026; £22.234m capital borrowing planned for 2026/27; £31.410m total capital expenditure in 2026/27 vs £21.798m in 2025/26

findings.paper_title: Main Report - Budget and Council Tax 2026-27 - Full Council
findings.headline: Unfunded homelessness grant cut of £81k forces increased use of reserves
findings.detail: Despite MHCLG assurances that no council would see cuts, Swale lost £81k in homelessness funding with no mitigation. This is rare: only 3 councils nationally affected (including Thanet in Kent). The council has written to MHCLG but has updated the budget to assume increased use of reserves to cover the gap.
findings.matters: The council is burning reserves to cover a funding cut outside its control. This reduces financial flexibility for real pressures and represents a loss of autonomy in reserve management.
findings.figures: £81k reduction; only 3 councils in the country affected
findings.quote: Swale has seen a reduction of £81k of homelessness funding with no further mitigation to address the loss. I have written to MHCLG asking for their position of no change in total allocations to be honoured and have been advised that this is being looked into. Further investigation by Kent Finance Officers has confirmed that there are only 3 councils in the country that have seen a cut in the homelessness grant with Thanet also affected in Kent. We will be following up with MHCLG with the aim of receiving additional funding, but the budget has been updated to assume an increase in the use of reserves.

findings.headline: Revenue Support Grant falls from £8.062m (2026/27) to £7.948m (2027/28) and £7.791m (2028/29) after business rate pooling change
findings.detail: A change to how business rate pool growth is shared has materially cut Swale's RSG. Government has provided a one-off Adjustment Support Grant (£1.223m) to protect 2026/27, but this expires in 2027/28. The director explicitly states the budget gap forecast for future years increases significantly as a result, with no certainty on government action.
findings.matters: This is a structural funding loss, not a one-off issue, and signals material budget stress from 2027/28 onwards when the protection expires. A lender needs to know the council faces a cliff edge in grant funding.
findings.figures: Adjustment Support Grant £1.223m (2026/27 only), then £0. Revenue Support Grant falls from £8.062m in 2026/27 forecast to £7.948m in 2027/28 and £7.791m in 2028/29.
findings.quote: the change to the assumption on how Business Rate Pools share business rate growth has significantly reduced the Revenue Support Grant allocation for Swale and as the Adjustment Support Grant is a one off protection arrangement for 2026/27 the budget gap forecast for future years increases significantly

findings.headline: Leisure Centre Improvements will require £2m borrowing in 2026/27, stepping up from £287k in 2025/26.
findings.detail: Leisure capital spending accelerates from £287k in 2025/26 to £2m in 2026/27, both funded by borrowing. No further spending is planned in 2027/28, suggesting a discrete, time-limited capital project.
findings.matters: Major capital investment in discretionary services (leisure) signals the council's assessment of borrowing headroom and priorities; discretionary assets are typically vulnerable to deferral if financial pressures emerge, so large commitments reflect current financial confidence.

findings.headline: Council is borrowing £1.37m to purchase temporary accommodation in 2025/26, indicating housing demand pressure.
findings.detail: A dedicated capital scheme for temporary accommodation purchases via borrowing suggests demand for temporary housing exceeds existing council stock. The scheme does not continue in later years, indicating an immediate, one-off capital response.
findings.matters: Growth in temporary accommodation is a leading indicator of housing stress in the area and typically creates ongoing revenue pressure (temporary housing costs more per unit than permanent solutions), affecting financial sustainability and budget forecasts.

findings.headline: Local Housing Company capital spending will require £20.1m net borrowing in 2026/27, concentrated in a single year.
findings.detail: The scheme shows zero activity in 2025/26, then steps up to £21.062m spend in 2026/27 with only £969k income recovery, leaving net borrowing of £20.093m. This drops to zero in 2027/28, suggesting a time-limited capital commitment, likely for housing stock acquisition or development.
findings.matters: A £20m borrowing requirement in a single year materially affects debt profiles and borrowing capacity. This scheme alone represents 64% of the council's total net capital spending in 2026/27 (£31.4m), signalling significant housing investment and debt take-on.

findings.paper_title: App I - SBC Audit Findings Report 2024-25
findings.headline: IFRS 16 implementation incomplete: three finance leases totalling £134k not yet reclassified to right-of-use assets
findings.detail: Auditors identified 10 finance leases (£1.75m net book value) that should have been reclassified to Right-of-Use assets under IFRS 16 at 1 April 2024. Seven were subsequently corrected following auditor discussion, but three assets totalling £134,367 in Land and Buildings and Community Infrastructure Assets remain to be reclassified, with management committing to action this in 2025/26.
findings.matters: Incomplete implementation of mandatory accounting standards indicates gaps in the council's control environment and financial reporting processes, with adjustments likely needed in the following year.
findings.figures: Three uncorrected lease assets £134,367; total identified leases £1.75m
findings.quote: We identified 10 finance leases classified under Land and Buildings (L&B) and community assets with a net book value of £1.75m that were not reclassified to Right-of-Use (RoU) assets on transition to IFRS 16. Following our discussion with management, 7 out of the 10 were reclassified. Three remaining assets of £134,367 under Land and buildings, Community and Infrastructure Assets are yet to be reclassified. Management confirmed these will be reclassified during 2025/26.

findings.paper_title: App I - SBC Audit Findings Report 2024-25
findings.headline: Prior year £2.085m accounting error from 2023/24 disclosed in 2024/25 comparatives without correction in original year
findings.detail: The 2023/24 audit identified a £2.085m prior period adjustment where expenditure relating to Kent County Council was incorrectly recorded as Property Plant and Equipment instead of Revenue Expenditure Funded from Capital Under Statute (REFCUS). This should have been expensed. Management chose not to adjust the 2023/24 financial statements at the time, resulting in that year's accounts being qualified. The error now appears as a comparator in 2024/25.
findings.matters: A significant accounting error that was known but not corrected demonstrates management was willing to accept material misstatement in the prior year, raising concerns about the rigour of the council's financial controls and accounting processes.
findings.figures: £2.085m prior period adjustment
findings.quote: The prior year error was a £2.085m prior period adjustment where expenditure relating to Kent County Council was recorded as Property Plant and Equipment instead of Revenue Expenditure Funded from Capital Under Statute (REFCUS) and should have been expensed. Management had chosen not to adjust the 2023/24 financial statements.

findings.paper_title: App I - SBC Audit Findings Report 2024-25
findings.headline: Audit opinion to be qualified due to material misstatement of prior year comparative arising from PPE disposal accounting
findings.detail: The auditor intends to issue an 'Except for' Qualification on the 2024/25 financial statements because a disposal of Property, Plant and Equipment was incorrectly processed during 2023/24 balances instead of being restated via opening balances. This is a material misstatement of the comparative figures. The same issue contributed to the 2023/24 accounts being qualified.
findings.matters: A qualified audit opinion signals control and financial reporting weaknesses, indicating the council's accounting systems may not reliably capture all transactions or may have gaps in the approval and classification process that creditors need to understand.
findings.figures: Material misstatement of comparative in 2024/25 financial statements
findings.quote: Our anticipated financial statements audit report opinion will be modified. We intend to issue an 'Except for' Qualification on the 2024/25 financial statements due to a material misstatement of the comparative arising from the accounting treatment of the disposal of an item of Property, Plant, and Equipment which should have been processed via a restatement of Opening Balances as opposed to it being transacted during the 2023/24 balances.

findings.headline: A 2023-24 improvement recommendation to map corporate risks to strategic objectives remains unaddressed after one year.
findings.detail: The auditor recommended in 2023-24 that the Council map risks identified in the Corporate Risk Register to the strategic objectives in the corporate plan. This recommendation was included to improve member visibility of which strategic priorities are most vulnerable to risk. As of March 2025, there is no evidence this has been implemented.
findings.matters: Unaddressed audit recommendations, especially when repeated, indicate either weak governance execution or capacity constraints. This pattern raises questions about the council's ability to implement management actions.
findings.figures: None
findings.quote: A previous recommendation to map risks to strategic objectives remains outstanding, and we continue to advise its implementation to improve Member oversight. However, there is no evidence of this recommendation being addressed.

findings.headline: A prior-year accounting error of £2.085m from 2023-24 remains uncorrected, resulting in a modified audit opinion.
findings.detail: A £2.085m misclassification from 2023-24—where Kent County Council expenditure was incorrectly recorded as Property Plant and Equipment instead of Revenue Expenditure Funded from Capital Under Statute (REFCUS)—was not corrected in the prior year accounts. The council chose not to adjust the 2023-24 financial statements. This error remains in the comparatives and results in a modified audit opinion on the 2024-25 statements.
findings.matters: An unrecorrected material error suggests governance gaps in financial reporting quality. A lender needs to understand whether this reflects process weakness or inability to correct identified issues.
findings.figures: £2.085m prior period adjustment
findings.quote: The prior year error was a £2.085m prior period adjustment where expenditure relating to Kent County Council was recorded as Property Plant and Equipment instead of Revenue Expenditure Funded from Capital Under Statute (REFCUS) and should have been expensed. Management had chosen not to adjust the 2023-24 financial statements.

findings.headline: Planning Services overspent by £0.9m in 2024-25, requiring offset from temporary savings and late grants.
findings.detail: Despite the council achieving an overall £0.317m surplus, Planning Services reported a £0.9m overspend. This was absorbed through temporary service-level savings and late-arriving housing grants rather than underlying demand management.
findings.matters: Persistent overspends in a statutory service like planning suggest underlying demand or cost pressures that may recur. Using one-off grants to mask overspends is not a sustainable solution.
findings.figures: £0.9m overspend in Planning Services
findings.quote: A £0.9m overspend in Planning Services was offset by temporary savings and late housing grants.

findings.headline: Capital programme experienced a £14.7m underspend in 2024-25, predominantly from Local Housing Company project delays.
findings.detail: The Council's £23.6m capital budget saw a £14.7m underspend, with £12.5m attributable to delays in the Local Housing Company housebuilding projects. The unspent capital has been re-profiled into 2025-26, suggesting either project management challenges or market/delivery constraints affecting the council's housing delivery capacity.
findings.matters: Capital slippage at this scale indicates the Council may face delivery challenges with major infrastructure and housing schemes. For lenders, this signals execution risk on council-led projects and delayed income benefits.
findings.figures: £23.6m capital budget; £14.7m underspend; £12.5m from Local Housing Company delays
findings.quote: The capital budget of £23.6m saw a £14.7m underspend due largely (£12.5m) to Local Housing Company housebuilding project delays. Spend has been re-profiled into 2025-26.

findings.headline: The Council projects a £4.9m annual deficit by 2028-29 but has not adopted a formal long-term savings programme despite prior year recommendation.
findings.detail: The Medium-Term Financial Strategy highlights a forecast annual deficit of £4.9m by 2028-29. The Council continues to identify savings within service budgets annually, but there remains no formal long-term savings programme. The auditor reiterated this as an improvement recommendation, noting that savings of this scale typically require transformational change with dedicated governance structures. For 2025-26, the Council is meeting a £0.677m deficit through reserves.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand whether the council has a credible, structured plan to address its growing funding gap. Year-to-year budget patches without a multi-year savings strategy pose material sustainability risk.
findings.figures: £4.9m forecast annual deficit by 2028-29; £0.677m reserve drawdown in 2025-26 to balance budget
findings.quote: An annual forecast deficit of £4.9m by the end of the MTFS period to 2028-29 poses a challenge and, though strong planning and oversight support resilience, without a formal savings programme this will be a difficult challenge to meet.

news_drafts.headline: Swale's Cockleshell Walk scheme of 51 social rented homes moves to construction, part-funded by borrowing
news_drafts.lead:
Swale Borough Council's 51 new social rented homes at Cockleshell Walk have moved to construction, according to the annual report of its external auditor (the independent check on the council's accounts), presented to the Audit Committee on 14 October. The scheme is paid for from several sources: capital receipts (money from selling assets, including Section 106 funds paid by developers), Homes England grant funding, reserves, and prudential borrowing (borrowing the council judges it can afford to repay).

The auditor's report says the development reached construction after planning permission was granted and the land was formally appropriated for the purpose. Cockleshell Walk is the only one of the three original sites in the Swale Rainbow Homes Ltd affordable housing programme to have got that far. The other two sites remain paused. The report does not give a cost for the scheme or say how the funding divides between its sources.

The auditor sets the borrowing decision alongside the council's own forecast that its reserves (money it has put aside) will fall to £6.5m by 2029/30. The report notes that the council has not yet identified formal savings to close future gaps in its budget.
